source_text: Quae praestant nihilo magis nos totius mundi fragore terreri, quam si videremus tristis lupini silvam sonantem vel immundis suibus vel ventis irruentibus commoveri [n97] .
pass_a_gloss: Which grant that we are terrified by the crash of the whole world no more than if we were seeing a wood of sad lupine sounding or being moved by unclean swine or by rushing winds.
pass_b_english: They ensure that all the world’s uproar frightens us no more than the sight of a rustling stand of bitter lupines shaken by filthy pigs or gusts of wind. [Literary allusion: Virgil, Georgics 1.75–76.]

choices.why: Loaded word in Julian's Latin at this locus; English follows LS/Blaise range without copying NPNF.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
